original_title: A24 very sorry it hit Backrooms-inspired art with a copyright strike
summary_en: The indie studio A24 is facing backlash after issuing copyright strikes against fan art inspired by the viral horror phenomenon, The Backrooms. Director Kane Parsons has intervened, prompting a public apology and a pledge of support from the studio.
ai_analysis: This incident highlights the complex relationship between major studios and the internet's collaborative mythologies, posing a critical question about ownership in the age of viral content.

en.title: A24 Apologizes After Backrooms Fan Art Takedown Controversy
en.summary: The indie studio A24 is facing backlash after issuing copyright strikes against fan art inspired by the viral horror phenomenon, The Backrooms. Director Kane Parsons has intervened, prompting a public apology and a pledge of support from the studio.
en.body:
The internet's labyrinthine corridors, particularly those of online horror sensation **The Backrooms**, have become a battleground for intellectual property rights. **A24**, the studio behind the upcoming film adaptation, found itself in hot water this past weekend after reports surfaced of copyright strikes being issued against fan art. These takedown notices targeted creators selling works inspired by the iconic yellow-wallpaper aesthetic that birthed the collaborative universe.

Fans and creators alike voiced their outrage, with many pointing to the irony of a studio known for its auteur-driven, often unconventional films engaging in what felt like heavy-handed copyright enforcement against the very community that fostered the phenomenon. **Kane Parsons**, the young director of the **A24**-produced **Backrooms** film, quickly stepped in to address the controversy. He assured the community that he was investigating the matter, stating, "I’m looking into this. Should not be happening."

## A Studio's Statement Amidst the Chaos

Following **Parsons**' intervention and the growing community outcry, **A24** issued a statement acknowledging the misstep. The studio communicated its message via Instagram Stories, a platform known for its ephemeral nature, which itself drew some criticism. However, screenshots of the statement circulated widely, showing **A24** recognizing the expansive nature of **The Backrooms**' creative ecosystem.

> "The Backrooms is one part of an infinitely bigger ecosystem, rife with creatives who have every right to tell their own version of the story."

This admission suggests a course correction, with **A24** backtracking on the aggressive copyright enforcement and signaling a commitment to supporting the community creators who have been instrumental in building the **Backrooms** lore. The studio's swift response, prompted by **Parsons**' direct involvement, appears to have de-escalated the immediate conflict.

## The Wider Implications for Internet Culture

This kerfuffle is more than just a dispute over fan art; it underscores the delicate balance Hollywood is attempting to strike as it increasingly mines internet culture for content. While some online phenomena have clear origins and ownership, like **Trevor Henderson**'s Siren Head, **The Backrooms** began as an anonymous 4chan post, making its ownership inherently ambiguous. **A24**'s initial actions raised concerns about large corporations potentially stifling the organic creativity that birthed these digital myths. The swift reversal, however, indicates a growing understanding that these properties often thrive on community participation and adaptation, not strict control.

## What's Next for The Backrooms

With **A24** now publicly supporting the community, attention will likely shift to the development of **Kane Parsons**' film. Fans will be eager to see how the studio navigates future community engagement and whether this incident will set a precedent for how **A24** and other studios approach adapting internet-born properties. Details regarding the film's production and release are still emerging.

es.title: A24 se disculpa tras la polémica por el retiro de arte de fans de The Backrooms
es.summary: La productora A24 se enfrenta a críticas después de emitir órdenes de retiro de derechos de autor contra arte de fans inspirado en el fenómeno de terror en línea, The Backrooms. El director Kane Parsons interviene y la productora ofrece una disculpa pública y un compromiso de apoyo. La comunidad de fans y creadores se sintió ofendida por la decisión de A24, considerándola una medida excesiva y contradictoria con la esencia de la plataforma.
es.body:
Las complejas redes de internet, especialmente aquellas relacionadas con el fenómeno de terror en línea **The Backrooms**, se han convertido en un campo de batalla para los derechos de propiedad intelectual. **A24**, la productora detrás de la próxima adaptación cinematográfica, se vio envuelta en una controversia el fin de semana pasado después de que surgieron informes sobre órdenes de retiro de derechos de autor contra arte de fans. Estas notificaciones de retiro apuntaban a creadores que vendían obras inspiradas en la estética de papel pintado amarillo que dio origen al universo colaborativo.

 
## Un estudio en medio del caos
Los fans y creadores expresaron su indignación, muchos señalando la ironía de que una productora conocida por sus películas dirigidas por autores y a menudo poco convencionales, estuviera participando en lo que parecía ser una aplicación excesiva de los derechos de autor contra la propia comunidad que había alimentado el fenómeno. **Kane Parsons**, el joven director de la película **The Backrooms** producida por **A24**, intervino rápidamente para abordar la controversia. Aseguró a la comunidad que estaba investigando el asunto, declarando: "Estoy investigando esto. No debería estar sucediendo".

 
## Declaración de un estudio en medio del caos
Después de la intervención de **Parsons** y el creciente clamor de la comunidad, **A24** emitió un comunicado reconociendo el error. La productora comunicó su mensaje a través de Instagram Stories, una plataforma conocida por su naturaleza efímera, lo que en sí mismo generó algunas críticas. Sin embargo, capturas de pantalla del comunicado se difundieron ampliamente, mostrando a **A24** reconociendo la naturaleza expansiva del ecosistema creativo de **The Backrooms**.

 
> "The Backrooms es solo una parte de un ecosistema mucho más grande, lleno de creativos que tienen todo el derecho de contar su propia versión de la historia."

 
## Implicaciones más amplias para la cultura de internet
Esta disputa es más que una discusión sobre el arte de los fans; subraya el delicado equilibrio que Hollywood está tratando de mantener a medida que explora cada vez más la cultura de internet en busca de contenido. Mientras que algunos fenómenos en línea tienen orígenes y propiedad claros, como **Trevor Henderson**'s Siren Head, **The Backrooms** comenzó como una publicación anónima en 4chan, lo que hace que su propiedad sea inherentemente ambigua. Las acciones iniciales de **A24** generaron preocupaciones sobre cómo las grandes corporaciones podrían sofocar la creatividad orgánica que dio vida a estos mitos digitales. El rápido cambio de rumbo, sin embargo, indica una creciente comprensión de que estas propiedades a menudo prosperan gracias a la participación y adaptación de la comunidad, y no a través de un control estricto.

 
## Próximos pasos para The Backrooms
Con **A24** ahora apoyando públicamente a la comunidad, es probable que la atención se centre en el desarrollo de la película de **Kane Parsons**. Los fans estarán ansiosos por ver cómo la productora navega el compromiso con la comunidad en el futuro y si este incidente sentará un precedente para cómo **A24** y otras productoras abordan la adaptación de propiedades nacidas en internet. Los detalles sobre la producción y el lanzamiento de la película aún están emergiendo.

content_raw: A24 issued a statement this weekend addressing claims that it was getting heavy-handed with copyright strikes against online creators working in the world of online horror sensation The Backrooms, acknowledging that Kane Parson’s film set in the collaborative universe, Backrooms , “is one part of an infinitely bigger ecosystem.” (We’d link directly to said statement, but the studio made the irritating decision to issue it via its Instagram Story, the self-destructing Mission: Impossible  tape of modern social media communication; outlets like  Kotaku  have screenshots of the statement .) The statement arrived a few days after a Reddit post went viral , stating that an artwork being sold on Redbubble, based on the yellow wallpaper designs from the original Backrooms images that inspired the meme, had been hit with a takedown request. Parsons himself posted a response in the thread, saying “I’m looking into this. Should not be happening”; Discord messages allegedly sent by him in the aftermath included statements that he was “pressuring” the studio to discontinue any such efforts.  As we’ve noted before , this latest kerfuffle is of a piece with the tricky place that copyright and ownership hold as Hollywood studios start making serious efforts to mine memes and other socially spread ideas for successful films. While some online cryptids do have a specific provenance—including Trevor Henderson’s Siren Head, which is being developed for a film at Warner Bros. by Zach Cregger and Brian Duffield —many more are like The Backrooms, which started life as a series of anonymous posts on 4chan, and can’t be credibly claimed to be “owned” by anybody. Sure, individual creators—notably Parsons, who became the most successful Backrooms-adjacent filmmaker while still just a teenager—have made their own works in the universe, and put their own spins on its liminal spaces mythos. But part of the appeal of these memes has always been that they’re a playground anyone with a camera/Blender/game development tools can mess around in, with no one worrying about who owns what. In its statement, A24 acknowledged the Redbubble takedown, saying it was submitted as an automated claim. “We immediately began the process to reverse it and reinstate the listing,” the studio’s PR team wrote. The statement went on to assert that “A24 makes no claim of ownership over the yellow wallpaper, the original post referencing it, or any of the community works that have since been built around it. We will continue to support the artists who, like Kane, were inspired by it.”
